chapter.title: Tutorial
chapter.para: This chapter is a hands-on introduction to Scaly. It gets you from an empty file to a running program, then takes you on a quick tour of the language. Later chapters cover everything here in depth; the goal now is to write and run real code as fast as possible.

section.title: Building the Compiler from the Seed
section.para: Scaly is self-hosted: the compiler is written in Scaly and compiles itself. It is distributed as a seed — the compiler emitted as its own LLVM IR, the .ll files committed under seed/ (one set per target platform). Turning the seed back into a working scalyc needs only LLVM 18 and a C compiler for the final link; no C++ toolchain is involved.
Install the prerequisites, then run the build script from the repository root:
section.programlisting:
; macOS brew install llvm@18
; Ubuntu 24.04 sudo apt install llvm-18 clang-18
section.para: This compiles the seed with llc, links it into scalyc/build/scalyc, and builds the small runtime archive the compiler links your programs against. For brevity, the rest of this tutorial assumes the compiler is on your PATH:

note.para: The runtime archive lives at /tmp/libscaly.a. If it gets cleared — for example after a reboot — and the compiler reports it missing, just re-run tools/build-from-seed.sh to rebuild it.

section.para: The C++ bootstrap that originally produced the seed is described in ; you do not need it for everyday use.

section.title: A Tour of Scaly
section.para: This section sweeps quickly across the language using small, complete programs. If something is not fully explained here, do not worry — every feature is covered in detail in the rest of this specification, and each part of the tour points you to the relevant chapter.

section.title: Values and Bindings
section.para: Bind a value to a name with let. There is no equals sign — the name is followed directly by its value. Use var for a binding you intend to change, and set to change it. A semicolon starts a comment.
section.programlisting: let answer 42 ; immutable binding var count 0 ; mutable binding set count: count + 1 ; assignment uses a colon
section.para: The equals sign = is reserved for comparison, so it never gets confused with assignment. See for the full lexical rules.

section.title: Operators and Precedence
section.para: Operators are ordinary identifiers, not keywords baked into the grammar. When they are chained, they combine using standard mathematical precedence — multiplication binds tighter than addition:
section.programlisting: ; 3 + 4 * 5 is 3 + 20, which is 23 — not 35 let result 3 + 4 * 5 if result = 23 print("got 23") else print("unexpected")
section.para: Parentheses group explicitly, and an operator written before its operand acts as a prefix function (-x, ~flag). See for the complete model.

section.title: Control Flow
section.para: if chooses between branches. Single-statement branches need no braces; the condition needs no parentheses:
section.programlisting: let n 7 if n < 0 print("negative") else if n = 0 print("zero") else print("positive")
section.para: while repeats as long as its condition holds. Use braces for a multi-statement body:
section.programlisting: var sum 0 var i 1 while i <= 10 { set sum: sum + i set i: i + 1 } ; sum is now 55
section.para: for iterates. for i in 4 runs i from 0 up to — but not including — 4:
section.programlisting: var total 0 for i in 4 set total: total + i ; total is 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 6

section.title: Functions
section.para: A function declares its parameter types and return type. The value of the last expression is returned automatically — no return keyword is needed for the final result. A single-expression body needs no braces:
section.programlisting:
function add(a: int, b: int) returns int a + b
let s add(3, 4) ; s is 7
section.para: Functions can call themselves. Here is the classic factorial:
section.programlisting:
function factorial(n: int) returns int if n <= 1 1 else n * factorial(n - 1)
let f factorial(5) ; f is 120
section.para: Functions are pure: they read their arguments and return a value, with no side effects. To mutate, use a procedure.

section.title: Procedures and Mutation
section.para: A procedure is like a function but may change its inputs and perform side effects. The distinction is visible at every call site, so a reader always knows which calls can mutate state. See for the details.

section.title: Unions, Options, and choose
section.para: A union holds one of several variants. Each variant may carry a payload. The most common union is Option, which represents a value that may be absent:
Match on a union with choose. Each when clause names a binding, then the variant, then the result; the binding is bound to the variant's payload. An else clause handles the remaining variants:
section.programlisting:
function or_zero(o: Option) returns int choose o when v: Some v else 0
let a or_zero(Option.Some(7)) ; a is 7 let b or_zero(Option.None) ; b is 0
section.para: See for union layout, the T? shorthand, and pattern matching in full.

section.title: Putting It Together
section.para: Let us combine the pieces into one small, complete program: a safe division that returns an Option instead of crashing on a zero divisor, with the caller deciding what to print.
Start with the function. It returns None when the divisor is zero, and Some with the quotient otherwise:
section.programlisting:
define Option union(Some: int, None)
function safe_divide(a: int, b: int) returns Option if b = 0 Option.None else Option.Some(a / b)
section.para: Now call it and react to the result with choose. The Some arm receives the quotient; the else arm handles division by zero:
section.programlisting: let result safe_divide(20, 4) choose result when q: Some if q = 5 print("20 / 4 = 5") else print("unexpected quotient") else print("cannot divide by zero")
section.para: Put both pieces in divide.scaly, then build and run it:
It prints:
Change the call to safe_divide(7, 0) and the same program prints cannot divide by zero — the union makes the failure a value you must handle, not a crash you can forget.
From here, the rest of this specification fills in the details: the rules, the full model, and the system including generics, lifetimes, and region-based memory management.
